political.label: Political history
political.description: Examines institutions, diplomacy and struggles over power through different methods. Namier reconstructs parliamentary connections; Benson studies voters; Tilly investigates collective claims; Hunt joins political symbols and social identities. Hill, Dorothy Thompson and Flexner examine radical and rights politics, while Guha and Cooper investigate insurgency and labor under colonial rule. These approaches overlap without replacing all earlier political history.
political.representative_figures_and_works: Ranke is one major nineteenth-century root. Later examples: Lewis Namier, Charles Tilly, and Lynn Hunt’s Politics, Culture, and Class (1984). Further contexts: Namier (1929), Flexner (1959), William Appleman Williams (1959), Hill (1972), Guha (1983), Tilly (1986) and Cooper (1996).

strands.title: The new political history of Britain, 1993–2011
strands.focus: After the Social History round on Stedman Jones (1992–93), British political history took the linguistic turn and argued with it. Vernon's Politics and the People (1993) held that between the Reform Acts 'the official political subject was redefined in the image of print' and the public sphere narrowed (p. 107, as quoted by Tilly); his Re-reading the Constitution (1996) gathered Epstein, Wahrman, Joyce, Antony Taylor and Anna Clark under 'new narratives'. Vernon credited Epstein's late-1980s articles, subsequently collected in Radical Expression (1994), as inspirational 'for those like myself who followed into the field' of 'the new cultural history of British politics' (2004). Lawrence and Taylor's Party, State and Society (1997) set out to 'examine critically "electoral sociology"' (as quoted by LoPatin), and Lawrence's Speaking for the People (1998) questioned 'the rise of class politics' and 'the triumph of party' for the politics of place and gender; Vernon found it 'ambitious, but ultimately flawed' (1999) and Lawrence answered, in a response posted in 2010, that 'realist' and 'constructivist' approaches must be combined. Electing Our Masters (2009) followed the hustings and the platform; in 2011 Lawrence argued for a 'conservative' rather than 'liberal' modernity. Positions within one field, not a school; the debate entry languages_of_class holds the exchanges.
strands.works: Vernon, Politics and the People (1993), ed., Re-reading the Constitution (1996); Epstein, Radical Expression (1994); Lawrence and Taylor, eds, Party, State and Society (1997); Lawrence, Speaking for the People (1998), Electing Our Masters (2009), 'Paternalism, Class, and the British Path to Modernity' (2011); Vernon's review and Lawrence's response (Reviews in History, 1999/2010)

strands.title: Circulation and the politics of value
strands.focus: Following exchanged things connects valuation to social and political relations; Appadurai explicitly develops a resource from Simmel.
strands.works: The Social Life of Things (1986), introduction

strands.title: Cultural biographies and changing commodity status
strands.focus: A thing’s commodity status can change over time or differ between people; material production alone does not settle its social classification.

strands.title: Goods as social communication
strands.focus: Douglas and Isherwood examine goods as an information system through which people conduct social relations.

strands.title: Taste and social position
strands.focus: Read tastes and cultural practices in relation to social position, alongside approaches centered on circulation or household provisioning.

strands.title: Gendered consumption, work and identity
strands.focus: Investigate the division of family labor, male and female consumer identities, class differences and state definitions; avoid one universal consumer.

strands.title: Inventory evidence and its boundaries
strands.focus: Weatherill records selected goods across probate inventories. Missing laborers, debts, real estate and reliable clothing values constrain what household ownership can establish about society.

strands.title: Purchasing as household work
strands.focus: Vickery’s selected households distribute purchasing tasks and authority unevenly. Expenditure diaries show practical expertise, but incomplete income records limit reconstruction of financial power.
strands.works: The Gentleman’s Daughter (1998), “Elegance” opening and notes15–18

strands.title: Material meanings and unequal possibilities
strands.focus: Vickery finds social ambition alongside attachment and remembrance. Age, resources and inheritance matter; her chapter does not establish one feminine attitude to possessions.

strands.title: Competing chronologies and questions
strands.focus: Compare McKendrick’s eighteenth-century acceleration, Weatherill’s earlier middling ownership and de Vries’s household labor argument. Vickery questions universal motives. Different evidence and outcomes do not yield one automatic date for a consumer society.
strands.works: McKendrick (1982), introduction; Weatherill (1996), preface; de Vries (1994); Vickery (1998)

strands.title: Ming consumers and social distinctions
strands.focus: Clunas reads Wen Zhenheng’s judgments about appropriate objects as elite distinctions, then compares them with Yan Song’s confiscation inventory. These are different sources, not interchangeable records of actual purchasing.

strands.title: Whose consumption becomes visible?
strands.focus: Clunas’s selected texts privilege elite men. Rules assigning objects to women do not directly recover women’s own meanings; subsistence consumers also remain poorly represented. Pagani highlights this limit while praising the method.

strands.title: Relics and changing value
strands.focus: Geary follows transfers and renewed authentication of relics. Their careers may change how communities value them; price equivalences and the relative frequency of different transfers remain uncertain.

strands.title: Specific historical uses of theory
strands.focus: Vickery explicitly uses Bourdieu and Douglas/Isherwood; Geary cites Kopytoff. These establish particular uses with different evidence and questions, without proving uniform reception across consumption history.

strands.title: Luxury and European consumer culture
strands.focus: Berg and Clifford coedit a volume on luxury and consumer culture in Europe, 1650–1850. This records their editorial contribution; detailed chapter arguments remain unchecked.

spatialhistory.label: Spatial history / Historical geography
spatialhistory.date_label: Sauer 1925 · Hoskins 1955 · critical spatial studies and historical GIS by the 1990s
spatialhistory.description: Investigates how places, landscapes, territories and spatial relationships are made and transformed through time. Reconstructing past geographies, interpreting maps and colonial naming, tracing contested place identities, and linking historical records through GIS are different practices within this broad field.

spatialhistory.scope_note: Historical geography has roots well before digital mapping. Spatial history is an overlapping set of approaches, not a synonym for GIS or one unified school. The existing Geography & environmental inquiry entry retains its wider intellectual resources. This selection foregrounds British reconstruction, Australian colonial space and a British HGIS project; wider regional traditions and Indigenous spatial knowledge require fuller treatment. Later digital projects are not backdated into the period reviewed through 2000.

strands.title: Landscape reconstruction and historical traces
strands.focus: Sauer’s morphological programme and Hoskins’s landscape reading offer distinct ways of studying past environments.

strands.title: Reconstructing geography from historical records
strands.focus: Darby works from Domesday evidence; the extent of a source is not identical to the geography of a whole society.

strands.title: Maps as historical representations
strands.focus: Harley asks how power, rhetoric and conventions enter mapmaking. His argument supplies source criticism, not a reason to abandon spatial measurement.

strands.title: Contested places and their pasts
strands.focus: Massey’s relational account appears alongside Driver and Samuel’s spatial-history editorial; co-publication does not imply one shared theory.

strands.title: Colonial naming and spatial narratives
strands.focus: Carter examines Australian territorial representation; this analysis must remain distinct from Indigenous authority over Country.

strands.title: Urban landscapes and public interpretation
strands.focus: Hayden links material places with histories of diverse urban lives.

strands.title: Producing space through social practice and power
strands.focus: Lefebvre’s 1974 introduction asks how spaces and their codes are produced and changed through social practices, planning and power. Space participates in these relations rather than merely containing them. This is his theoretical proposal; the excerpt neither supplies a GIS procedure nor establishes a uniform school of spatial historians.
strands.works: La production de l’espace (1974), introduction excerpt pp. 19–27; The Production of Space, trans. Donald Nicholson-Smith (1991, metadata only)

strands.title: Uneven sovereignty: legal corridors and enclaves
strands.focus: Benton follows the relation between geographic descriptions, mobile subjects and delegated jurisdiction. Imperial space appears as differentiated corridors and enclaves; her account asks how these arrangements changed rather than treating all places as equally controlled or every legal anomaly as a temporary failure. The book’s full cases and later chapters remain unread here.
strands.works: A Search for Sovereignty (2010 imprint), introduction pp. 1–5 and 7–10; Humanity interview (2011), selected Benton answers.
